documents.title: ILAE classification of the epilepsies position paper

chunks.content: 1 Introduction Post‐stroke epilepsy (PSE) contributes to a substantial proportion of epilepsy burden, especially in older adults, where it accounts for half of all the new epilepsy cases [ ]. Our population is rapidly aging. Substantial effort has, therefore, been made in the last decade to create prognostic PSE models. The two most used predictive models for individualized PSE prognostication are the CAVE score for intracerebral hemorrhage (ICH) and the SeLECT score for ischemic stroke [ , ]. The SeLECT score includes five predictors: severity of stroke (NIHSS), large‐artery atherosclerosis etiology, early seizure (</ = 7 days), cortical involvement, and territory of the middle cerebral artery (MCA) [ ]. It was developed and validated in a European cohort. While several iterations of the SeLECT score have been published, we lack large‐scale studies to validate and improve the SeLECT score in geographically diverse populations, especially in the United States [ ]. A major barrier to applying the SeLECT score in large datasets is the need to manually extract MCA and cortical involvement from neuroimaging or clinical notes. These features are not routinely or consistently coded and require expert review of imaging or detailed electronic health records (EHRs) chart review. Recent neuroimaging research on lesion mapping found that the volume of post‐stroke chronic encephalomalacia is strongly associated with epilepsy development [ ]. Acute neuroimaging data for the CAVE score found ICH volume to be a significant predictor of epilepsy development when it is more than 10 mL [ ]. However, the SeLECT model did not consider the role of volume of acute ischemic stroke in PSE and only included two binary neuroimaging predictors (cortical and MCA territory involvement) [ , ]. Advances in machine learning and artificial intelligence have allowed automated tools for calculating ischemic stroke volumes using diffusion‐weighted imaging (DWI) [ , ]. The goal of our study was to determine if the size of acute ischemic stroke is a significant predictor of PSE and if its use can help overcome the limitation of manual extraction of neuroimaging data used in the SeLECT score. 2 Methods After institutional review board approval, we conducted a retrospective, single‐center study at the Cleveland Clinic in Cleveland, OH, USA. The study included adults with acute stroke admissions from January 2013 to October 2018, and DWI data from acute Magnetic Resonance Imaging (MRI). Cortical and MCA territory involvement was independently extracted by two board‐certified neurologists (VD and VP). Disagreements were mutually resolved. We obtained data on each variable of the SeLECT score through manual extraction from the EHRs. Patients without an MRI during admission or insufficient data to calculate the SeLECT score were excluded. Using these variables, we computed the SeLECT score for each patient in our sample. Clinical seizures during hospital admission and follow‐up, determined and documented in the EHR by a licensed healthcare provider, were extracted. A clinical seizure within ≤7 days of stroke was classified as an acute symptomatic seizure (ASyS), and a seizure > 7 days after stroke was classified as a PSE [ ]. 2.1 MRI Acquisition Clinically acquired MRIs were obtained retrospectively through the Picture Archiving and Communication System. Axial diffusion‐weighted echo planar images, including b = 0 and trace (b‐value = 1000 s/mm 2 ), were used to calculate the ischemic stroke volume. The sequence median (interquartile range [IQR]) parameters were echo time = 114 (98, 114) ms, repetition time = 3802 (3500, 4200) ms, in‐plane pixel resolution = 1.8 (1.7, 1.8) mm, and slice thickness = 7.0 (7.0, 7.0) mm. 2.2 DWI Analysis The training datasets came from a separate cohort of 175 patients with their first acute ischemic stroke, incomplete outcomes, or missing baseline MRI [ ]. The b0 and trace images were used to segment regions of hyperintense areas on trace images. For the training and validation, we manually segmented hyperintense DWI regions with consultation with a neuroradiologist (Appendix Figure ). The median DWI volume (IQR) was 3.0 (0.8−10.3) mL. We developed a convolutional neural network with a 2D U‐Net architecture [ ]. Briefly, the architecture had six levels with skip connections, and each unit with convolutions and batch normalization layers. The data were split into training, validation, and testing sets as a 5:1:1 ratio. The mean Dice coefficient on the validation dataset was 0.87, and the testing dataset was 0.81, which was within a typical range [ ]. The Dice similarity coefficient score is a statistical measure used to quantify the spatial overlap between two binary segmentations, typically, the automated segmentation output and the ground truth manual segmentation, of stroke lesions in neuroimaging studies [ ]. As a post‐processing, we used the b0 and trace images to calculate the maps of apparent diffusion coefficients (ADCs), and the hypointense ADC areas were retained if the lesion‐wise 25th percentile ADC value was smaller than 600×10 −6 mm

mean Dice coefficient on the validation dataset was 0.87, and the testing dataset was 0.81, which was within a typical range [ ]. The Dice similarity coefficient score is a statistical measure used to quantify the spatial overlap between two binary segmentations, typically, the automated segmentation output and the ground truth manual segmentation, of stroke lesions in neuroimaging studies [ ]. As a post‐processing, we used the b0 and trace images to calculate the maps of apparent diffusion coefficients (ADCs), and the hypointense ADC areas were retained if the lesion‐wise 25th percentile ADC value was smaller than 600×10 −6 mm 2 /s and if the lesion size is 4 voxels or greater with an 18‐connectivity. The results were visually checked by a rater and modified if necessary. For external validation, we applied the model to the Ischemic Stroke Lesion Segmentation 2022 (ISLES22) training dataset, consisting of 250 studies [ ]. Briefly, ISLES22 included subjects 18 years or older who had received MR imaging of the brain for previously diagnosed or suspected stroke. The MRI protocols included FLAIR and DWI trace images at a b‐value of up to 1000 s/mm 2 , as well as an ADC map at a 2 mm isotropic resolution. The zero‐shot validation showed a median Dice (IQR) of 0.65 (0.38, 0.76). However, the median (IQR) DWI lesion volume in ISLES 22 was 6.66 (1.58, 21.2) mL, which was larger than the internal training dataset ( t ‐test, p <0.001). After the model was fine‐tuned to ISLES22, the Dice improved to 0.82 (0.65, 0.88). 2.3 Statistical Analysis Descriptive statistics were computed for the entire cohort and stratified by whether the patient developed PSE. Mean with standard deviation or median with IQR was used for continuous variables, and frequency with percentage was used for categorical variables. Comparisons were made using two‐sample t ‐tests or Wilcoxon rank sum tests for continuous variables and Fisher's exact test for categorical variables. We first applied the published point‐based SeLECT score to our cohort [ ]. Then, we refit the SeLECT model in our cohort by re‐estimating the coefficients of its original predictors using a multivariable Cox proportional hazards model with time to PSE as the outcome. This allowed us to assess how the published SeLECT model performed in our data and to compare it with both the refit model and the additional models we developed. Patients who did not develop PSE were censored at their last follow‐up date. The proportional hazards assumption was evaluated using Schoenfeld residuals, and no major violations were detected. We then fit various models by adding stroke volume and then removing one or both of cortical involvement and MCA. Stroke volume was modeled as a continuous variable (per 10 mL). Nonlinearity was examined visually, and no major deviations from linearity were observed. Therefore, the total number of models that were fit includes the following: Refit SeLECT model (NIHSS + LAA + early seizure + cortical involvement + MCA) SeLECT + stroke volume SeLECT + stroke volume—cortical involvement SeLECT + stroke volume—MCA SeLECT + stroke volume—cortical involvement—MCA For each of these models, we compared discrimination using the concordance index (C‐index). Model calibration was examined graphically. We internally validated each of these models using bootstrapping with 500 iterations. To determine whether the optimism‐corrected C‐index was different between models, we used bootstrapping with 1000 bootstrap samples to compute 95% confidence intervals for the difference between each pair of optimism‐corrected C‐index values. Furthermore, for clinical use purposes, we analyzed whether there was a stroke volume threshold beyond which the size of the stroke is significantly more predictive of PSE. Because time to PSE is a time‐dependent outcome, we performed time‐dependent receiver operating characteristic (ROC) analysis, where time to PSE was the dependent variable, and stroke volume was the predictor. Specifically, we used the cumulative sensitivity and dynamic specificity method [ ]. We created ROC curves for each of the 6‐month, 1‐year, and 2‐year periods, and the area under the ROC curve (AUC), along with a 95% confidence interval, was computed. The optimal cutoff point for stroke volume was determined at each time point using Youden's index (the maximum vertical distance from the ROC curve to the diagonal line) [ ]. The sensitivity, specificity, positive predictive value (PPV), and negative predictive value (NPV) at each time point, based on the corresponding stroke volume cutoff, were estimated. All computations were performed in R, version 4.3.1 [ ]. All tests were two‐sided, and statistical significance was defined as p < 0.05. 3 Results Of the 375 patients qualifying for the study criteria, 221 had both DWI data and data for all SeLECT variables and were included in the final analysis. Compared with the study cohort ( N = 221), excluded patients had significantly more frequent cortical involvement and higher NIHSS scores, resulting in higher SeLECT

specificity, positive predictive value (PPV), and negative predictive value (NPV) at each time point, based on the corresponding stroke volume cutoff, were estimated. All computations were performed in R, version 4.3.1 [ ]. All tests were two‐sided, and statistical significance was defined as p < 0.05. 3 Results Of the 375 patients qualifying for the study criteria, 221 had both DWI data and data for all SeLECT variables and were included in the final analysis. Compared with the study cohort ( N = 221), excluded patients had significantly more frequent cortical involvement and higher NIHSS scores, resulting in higher SeLECT scores (Appendix Table ). Representative examples of automated DWI lesion segmentation are shown in Figure . Cortical involvement on initial Computed Tomography (CT) is strongly associated with higher NIHSS [ , ]. The confirmation of stroke on the initial CT scan explains the lower likelihood of undergoing a subsequent MRI, leading to their exclusion from the current analysis. The mean age of the study cohort was 63.5 (±13.8) years and included 51% females. MRIs were acquired on Siemens systems in 96% of patients, with 93% from 1.5T scanners and the remainder from 3T scanners. During a median follow‐up of 59 months (IQR, 25–79), 35 (15.8%) patients developed PSE. Table shows descriptive statistics for the study cohort, stratified by their PSE status. On unadjusted analyses (Table ), patients who developed PSE had significantly higher SeLECT score, were more likely to have ASyS, and had larger stroke volume. Table shows the results of the models we examined. The original SeLECT score had a C‐index of 0.669 in our sample. Our refit SeLECT model had an optimism‐corrected C‐index of 0.642. Stoke volume remained an independently significant predictor of PSE in all models. Adding stroke volume to the SeLECT model resulted in an optimism‐corrected C‐index of 0.656. Keeping stroke volume while removing only cortical involvement or MCA territory resulted in an optimism‐corrected C‐index of 0.664 and 0.668, respectively. Keeping stroke volume but removing both cortical involvement and MCA resulted in an optimism‐corrected C‐index of 0.679. Table presents the differences in optimism‐corrected C‐index values for each pair of models, along with 95% confidence intervals. Given that all 95% confidence interval differences contained the null value of 0, we conclude that none of the models had significantly higher or lower optimism‐corrected C‐index values. Calibration was generally good for all models, as shown in Figure . Given that stroke volume is a statistically significant predictor in all models, we post hoc evaluated a threshold at which it becomes more predictive of PSE. Figure shows ROC curves for stroke volume at 6‐month, 1‐year, and 2‐year post‐stroke. Table shows the AUC, optimal stroke volume cutoff point, sensitivity, specificity, PPV, and NPV for each time point. AUC was higher for earlier time points. Stroke volume cutoff points varied by time point and ranged from 11.6 to 16.7 mL. 4 Discussion We found that acute stroke volume is a significant and independent predictor of PSE. There was a 12% increased risk of PSE for every 10 mL increase in stroke volume, which remained a significant predictor across all models. The predictive performance (discrimination and calibration) of the SeLECT model, when the stroke volume substitutes for both cortical and MCA involvement, was comparable to that of the original SeLECT score. This lack of significant difference in model performance, and stroke volume remaining a strong predictor across various models, suggests that it can reliably serve as a practical, automated proxy for the current neuroimaging components of the SeLECT score. Automated DWI‐based lesion segmentation has now become feasible and accurate, achieving a Dice coefficient in the range of 0.81−0.85 [ , ]. These methods are robust to variations in scanner type and image quality. They have been validated in multicenter cohorts [ , ]. Our DWI‐based volume analysis algorithm achieved a Dice coefficient on our internal dataset (0.87) and the external dataset (0.82), comparable to those of the Artifical Intelligence (AI) tools in the literature. Additionally, segmentation error is unlikely to bias our results meaningfully, as measurement error in stroke volume would tend to attenuate effect estimates rather than create spurious associations. Given the strong and consistent association across all models, the predictive value of stroke volume appears robust. The availability of open‐source, state‐of‐the‐art, and reliable tools for ischemic stroke volume calculation enables the calculation to be performed at scale for large datasets [ ]. In addition, researchers have developed validated, automated methods to extract NIHSS scores from EHRs using natural language processing [ ]. With both NIHSS and stroke volume now extractable at scale, most of the core predictors for PSE risk can be assembled without manual review, enabling efficient, reproducible, large‐scale research and clinical implementation. of stroke volume appears robust. The availability of open‐source, state‐of‐the‐art, and reliable tools for ischemic stroke volume calculation enables the calculation to be performed at scale for large datasets [ ]. In addition, researchers have developed validated, automated methods to extract NIHSS scores from EHRs using natural language processing [ ]. With both NIHSS and stroke volume now extractable at scale, most of the core predictors for PSE risk can be assembled without manual review, enabling efficient, reproducible, large‐scale research and clinical implementation. A very recent systematic review found that the SeLECT score's application in various geographical locations, including China, Turkey, and Japan, has limitations in its discrimination of PSE and is yet to be tested in an exclusively US population [ ]. Our study, to our knowledge, is the first application of the SeLECT score in a US cohort, demonstrating a more than 10% loss in its discriminatory power for predicting PSE (c‐index of 0.77 vs. 0.64) [ ]. This difference may reflect racial differences in PSE risk as shown in several extensive studies. The Northern Manhattan Study found that PSE risk was two ‐to three‐fold higher in Hispanics and non‐Hispanic Blacks compared to non‐Hispanic Whites [ ]. Similarly, the Cardiovascular Health Study and the Atherosclerosis Risk in Communities (ARIC) study have found a higher risk of PSE among Black participants, with risk factors like hypertension and diabetes exerting a more substantial effect in these minority populations [ , ]. When placed in the context of chronic lesional studies, our finding suggests that the volume of brain injury plays a critical role in epileptogenesis from the acute to the chronic pathological stages of stroke [ ]. It is noteworthy that, like the CAVE score, it seems that the minimum ischemic stroke volume that significantly increases PSE is more than 10 mL [ ]. Limitations of this study include the retrospective, single‐center approach. Additionally, more severe stroke patients and those with cortical involvement on CT scan did not receive MRI and hence, were excluded from the current analysis. To overcome this selection bias and increase the generalizability of the stroke volume as a robust PSE predictor, we plan to evaluate it using automated tools that use CT scans [ ]. Additionally, future multicenter studies with larger sample sizes are needed to validate our findings and create new prognostic models that utilize stroke volume to predict PSE [ ]. Overall, stroke volume provides a more precise and quantitative measure of acute brain injury than binary regional designations. Our findings indicate that automated DWI‐based volume estimation can serve as a practical alternative to manually abstracted cortical and MCA involvement. Automated segmentation is feasible and sufficiently accurate, and it substantially reduces the burden of manual data extraction. Incorporating stroke volume into prognostic modeling may enhance the efficiency and objectivity of PSE risk prediction and, with further validation, could become a preferred imaging‐based predictor. Funding The authors have nothing to report. Acknowledgments and Disclosure The authors have nothing to report. Conflicts of Interest The authors declare no conflicts of interest.

documents.title: ILAE position paper antiepileptic drug therapeutic monitoring

chunks.content: Background The selective synaptic vesicle protein 2A (SV2A) ligand brivaracetam has been approved as a seizure suppressant drug in Europe since 2016. Compared to its predecessor drug levetiracetam (LEV), BRV binds to the SV2A protein with a 15- to 30-fold greater affinity without simultaneous modulation of the AMPA receptor [ ]. With a significant reduction in seizures with additional treatment with BRV, various studies have demonstrated good overall tolerability of the new antiseizure medication (ASM) as well as a reduced occurrence of psychiatric undesirable drug effects such as depression and irritability compared to LEV [ , , , ]. The risks of neurodevelopmental disorders and congenital malformations during pregnancy with antiseizure medication such as levetiracetam or lamotrigine are considered to be relatively low [ ]. Due to significant fluctuations in serum levels, dosage adjustments are often necessary during pregnancy with lamotrigine and levetiracetam [ ]. Although an increase in prescriptions of newer ASM such as BRV can be observed [ ], little is known about the teratogenic effects of BRV and potential serum level fluctuations during pregnancy. In a retrospective multicenter study, Steinig et al. [ ] examined post-marketing effects like efficacy, retention and tolerability in 262 patients with epilepsy who received brivaracetam as add-on therapy. During the observation period, two pregnancies occurred while taking BRV. As soon as the pregnancy became known, antiseizure medication was switched back to levetiracetam in accordance with the guidelines. Both pregnancies continued after temporary use of BRV. In 2020, a first case series of three women with epilepsy treated with brivaracetam during pregnancy was reported by Paolini and colleagues: The daily dose of BRV intake ranged from 50 mg/d to 200 mg/d. While two patients received BRV as monotherapy, the third received lamotrigine (LTG) as a comedication. Minor congenital malformations such as infantile hemangioma, congenital dermal melanocytosis and ankyloglossia were observed in two of three children (see Table ). Navarro et al. [ ] reported the birth of a healthy child on BRV therapy during pregnancy in a patient with therapy-refractory juvenile myoclonic epilepsy. Landmark and colleagues [ ] reported three healthy births during pregnancy with brivaracetam in two patients with epilepsy: Whereas one patient received BRV in monotherapy, the other also received perampanel and lacosamide as comedication. During pregnancy, serum levels of BRV remained stable in both patients. While the serum levels of BRV in the umbilical cord of both twins of one patient were reported as comparable to the blood concentration of their mother as measured one hour after last dose intake (infant/mother ratios: 1.1), BRV serum level in the umbilical cord of another newborn was reported as low (infant/mother ratio: 0.18) compared to its mother´s level as measured 9.5 h hours after last dose intake (see Table ). Case report Here we report a 31-year-old right-handed female patient who presented with pregnancy while being treated with BRV and TPM. She had focal, non-aware seizures occurring several times per week. During the seizures, she felt tachycardia and dizziness and did not respond to speech. In her past medical history, the patient reported febrile seizures that had occurred at the age of 6 years and a traumatic brain injury at the age of 11 years. The patient was medically refractory to lamotrigine (LTG) and levetiracetam (LEV). Due to the diagnosis of drug-resistant epilepsy, presurgical video-EEG monitoring was performed in 2014 and right occipital lobe epilepsy was diagnosed. A 3-Tesla cMRI showed no evidence of epileptogenic lesions. The patient refused any operative procedure. Subsequently, various antiseizure medications were given due to inadequate seizure control or side effects, such as zonisamide (ZNS), topiramate (TPM), valproate (VPA), carbamazepine (CBZ), oxcarbazepine (OXC), perampanel (PER), gabapentin (GBP) and BRV. In December 2021, the patient reported that she was pregnant, and was already 17 weeks pregnant. She presented with BRV (200 mg/d) and TPM (200 mg/d) and a seizure frequency of one per day. Serum levels of antiseizure medications, taken approximately 6 h after the morning doses, were 2.91 mg/l for BRV and 4.7 mg/l for TPM. The patient was already taking folic acid supplementation daily during pregnancy (5 mg/d). There was no switch back to levetiracetam, as is usual during pregnancy, as the patient refused this due to ineffectiveness and intolerance to this medication in the past. Due to the advanced pregnancy, it was assumed that organogenesis had already been completed. After detailed explanation, we decided together to continue the previous antiseizure medication. We agreed on monthly outpatient follow-ups. During those, the serum levels of antiseizure medication were stable (see Table ). Since the patient was only able to attend appointments in the early afternoon, drug levels were taken 6 h after the last dose. Seizure frequency during pregnancy was unchanged. At week 39, the patient gave spontaneous birth to a healthy daughter (Apgar score: 9/10/10). 1.5 h

After detailed explanation, we decided together to continue the previous antiseizure medication. We agreed on monthly outpatient follow-ups. During those, the serum levels of antiseizure medication were stable (see Table ). Since the patient was only able to attend appointments in the early afternoon, drug levels were taken 6 h after the last dose. Seizure frequency during pregnancy was unchanged. At week 39, the patient gave spontaneous birth to a healthy daughter (Apgar score: 9/10/10). 1.5 h after the last intake of antiseizure medication, the serum levels in the umbilical cord blood were 1.97 mg/l for brivaracetam and 3.0 mg/l for topiramate. The serum ratio of BRV (infant/mother) was 0.58 and serum ratio of TPM was 0.56. One month after delivery, the patient presented to our outpatient clinic. Her serum level of BRV was relatively stable (3.32 mg/l) comparable to the serum levels during pregnancy, whereas the serum level of TPM increased (7.3 mg/l). Seizure frequency was unchanged. Eight months after delivery, the patient returned to our outpatient clinic. She had stopped breastfeeding 6 months after delivery. The daughter was healthy and appropriately developed. BRV and TPM were still taken with unchanged daily dosage. Due to recent data on the increased risk of carcinoma with daily folic acid supplementation of more than 1 mg [ ], folic acid therapy was reduced to 0.8 mg daily. Discussion We report a 34-year-old patient with difficult-to-treat pharmacoresistant epilepsy who gave birth to a healthy child after pregnancy with topiramate and brivaracetam. Topiramate may be associated with an increased incidence of major congenital malformations: Based on data from 7355 pregnancies in the EURAP study group, Tomson and colleagues showed that 6 of 152 pregnancies (3.9%) with topiramate lead to major congenital malformation, such as cardiac malformation or hypospadias [ , ]. A review of the Cochrane database also showed that prenatal exposure to topiramate may lead to facial malformations [ ]. A systematic review by Schmidt and colleagues [ ] examining umbilical cord transmission of ASM found that antiseizure medication associated with an increased risk of congenital malformations, such as TPM, CBZ or VPA showed relevant differences among each other with respect to penetration into the fetal circulation. Regarding topiramate, the authors reported an intermediate penetration rate of topiramate into the umbilical cord with a comparatively high penetration of TPM into breast milk. Due to the risk of congenital malformations, fetal growth impairments and possible neuropsychiatric developmental disorders, the drug commission of the German medical association published a red hand letter in November 2023 with restrictions to prevent exposure to topiramate during pregnancy [ ]. Although an increasing use of newer ASM like SV2A ligand brivaracetam can be observed [ , ], evidence on newer antiseizure medication during pregnancy is scarce, particularly regarding therapeutic drug monitoring. The SV2A ligand brivaracetam is rapidly absorbed. According to previous evidence in healthy volunteers on BRV monotherapy, a dose-dependent peak in serum concentration is reached 2 h after ingestion with a plasma half-life of 9 h [ , , ]. To our knowledge the study by Landmark and colleagues [ ] is the first to provide pharmacokinetic data on brivaracetam in pregnancy and lactation. Landmark and colleagues determined serum concentrations 3 h after ingestion of 75 mg BRV (P1) and 9.5 h after ingestion of 100 mg BRV (P2). At P1 this was 0.81 mg/l. At P2 this was 1.4 mg/l. However, P2 was also on comedication with LCM and PER. The serum concentrations of BRV remained relatively stable in our patient, when 100 mg of BRV was taken twice daily. Since our patient was only able to attend appointments in the early afternoon, drug levels were taken at latest 6 h after the last dose intake. Compared to P1 in Landmark and colleagues, the concentration of BRV in our patient was higher despite a later blood sample. Compared to P2 in Landmark and colleagues, the concentration of BRV in the blood was also higher, with the same BRV dose but earlier blood sampling. Possible reasons for these results could be pharmacogenetic factors as well as metabolic influences of comedication with topiramate. Although there is little evidence regarding pregnancy and birth with newer ASM such as brivaracetam, the present case demonstrated that an uncomplicated pregnancy and healthy childbirth is possible. In a questionnaire-based survey, Mann and colleagues examined the knowledge of women with epilepsy (WWE) about their disease in a multicenter study between October and December 2020 and compared these results with data from 2005. Regarding disease-specific knowledge, there were no significant group differences in the cohort between 2005 and 2020. as metabolic influences of comedication with topiramate. Although there is little evidence regarding pregnancy and birth with newer ASM such as brivaracetam, the present case demonstrated that an uncomplicated pregnancy and healthy childbirth is possible. In a questionnaire-based survey, Mann and colleagues examined the knowledge of women with epilepsy (WWE) about their disease in a multicenter study between October and December 2020 and compared these results with data from 2005. Regarding disease-specific knowledge, there were no significant group differences in the cohort between 2005 and 2020. The authors found that special life events, like pregnancy in women with epilepsy, are associated with worries and false beliefs, which may lead to a reduction in ASM during pregnancy or a delayed medical consultation. The lack of knowledge correlated with lower educational level and with an elderly age. Due to the fact, that women with epilepsy are more likely to have unplanned pregnancies [ ], regular neurological-epileptological consultations should take place. In these, the change to ASM should be discussed regularly and in line with the patient`s prior knowledge if she wishes to have children. Furthermore, patients and their partners should be repeatedly informed, that a neurological consultation regarding a change or adjustment of the antiseizure medication should take place immediately after the pregnancy becomes known. Due to the fact, that half of epilepsies begin in childhood, the transition consultation should play a key role in providing information about epilepsy and pregnancy [ ]. In addition, interdisciplinary collaboration with gynecological colleagues should also be expanded. Finally, especially in the case of pregnancies under new antiseizure medications, reporting to pregnancy registries (e.g. EURAP) is necessary as well as an easier access to research databases [ ]. Conclusions Before or at latest when patients with ASM get pregnant, counselling should be performed by neurologist or epilepsy specialists to assess pharmacotherapy. Because there is little evidence regarding pregnancy with newer antiseizure medication, particularly regarding ASM concentrations, data donation to the pregnancy registries is important. Further data on the safety of brivaracetam during pregnancy are needed.
